entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5407"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 41</title> <div sID="gen8135" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.41.1-Job.41.34">Job 41:1-34</reference>.<div eID="gen8135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8136" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5407"/><hi type="bold">1. leviathan--</hi>literally, "the twisted animal," gathering itself in folds: a synonym to the Thannin (<reference osisRef="Job.3.8">Job 3:8</reference>, Margin; see <reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Psa 74:14</reference>; type of the Egyptian tyrant; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.26">Psa 104:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.1">Is 27:1</reference>; the Babylon tyrant). A poetical generalization for all cetacean, serpentine, and saurian monsters (see on <reference osisRef="Job.40.15">Job 40:15</reference>, hence all the description applies to no one animal); especially the crocodile; which is naturally described after the river horse, as both are found in the Nile.<div eID="gen8136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tongue ... lettest down?--</hi>The crocodile has no tongue, or a very small one cleaving to the lower jaw. But as in fishing the tongue of the fish draws the baited hook to it, God asks, Canst thou in like manner take leviathan?

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5417"/><div sID="gen8151" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5417"/><hi type="bold">11. prevented--</hi>done Me a favor first: anticipated Me with service (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.3">Psa 21:3</reference>). None can call Me to account ("stand before Me," <reference osisRef="Job.41.10">Job 41:10</reference>) as unjust, because I have withdrawn favors from him (as in Job's case): for none has laid Me under a prior obligation by conferring on Me something which was not already My own. What can man give to Him who possesses all, including man himself? Man cannot constrain the creature to be his "servant" (<reference osisRef="Job.41.4">Job 41:4</reference>), much less the Creator. <div eID="gen8151" type="x-p"/>

Translate: "his sneezing, causeth a light to shine." Amphibious animals, emerging after having long held their breath under water, respire by violently expelling the breath like one sneezing: in the effort the eyes which are usually directed towards the sun, seem to flash fire; or it is the expelled breath that, in the sun, seems to emit light.<div eID="gen8160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyelids of morning--</hi>The Egyptian hieroglyphics paint the eyes of the crocodile as the symbol for morning, because the eyes appear the first thing, before the whole body emerges from the deep [Horæ Hierogliphicæ 1.65.
